newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka says healthy economy is key to peace.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka says healthy economy is key to peace.

text.p: Sri Lanka, pushing ambitious political and economic reforms, said on Monday a healthy economy is the key to bringing peace and prosperity to this strife-torn island nation.

Deputy Finance Minister Gamini Lakshman Peiris, a senior member of President Chandrika Kumaratunga's reformist administration, said 1997 would be a landmark year as the government pursued political and economic change.
"The government is acutely conscious of the close relationship between economic reality and political reform," Peiris said in a speech in the capital, Colombo.

Peiris, who is also Constitutional Affairs Minister, said the kind of political change necessary to end Sri Lanka's ethnic war and usher in prosperity could only be possible once economic conditions had improved.
Kumaratunga, elected two years ago, is pursuing an ambitious strategy of economic and political reform aimed at ending the war with Tamil separatists and boosting economic growth.
She is seeking parliamentary and popular approval for constitutional changes that would devolve power to provinces, giving Tamils a high degree of autonomy.

Her peace plan has been rejected by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), the guerrilla force fighting for an independent homeland in the north and the east of this predominantly Sinhalese nation.
Kumaratunga also wants to end the executive presidency and introduce electoral reforms and guarantees of fundamental rights.

The government has also announced a package of tough spending cuts, increased revenue through wider tax compliance and a new goods and services tax, and a sell-off of government businesses, including stakes in the national airline, Air Lanka, and Sri Lanka Telecom.
Peiris said the government's economic reforms were aimed at boosting growth, which slowed to 3.7 percent in calendar 1996 from 5.5 percent the previous year.
Changes to the constitution must be approved by a national referendum and by at least two-thirds of the 225-seat parliament, where the government has only a one-seat majority.
"Now, all of this is going to be successful only if we are able to maintain a certain level of economic well-being and contentment in our country," Peiris said.

Peiris said there had been "a significant change in public opinion" as Sri Lankans accepted the need for change, including the government's plan to "empower the people in all parts of our country and lay the foundation for a durable and equitable settlement to this vexed problem".
The government says more than 50,000 people have died in the war, now in its 14th year. But the Tigers insist the death toll is much higher.
